We present a comparative analysis of photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk breeze models for the TW Hydrae protoplanetary disk, utilizing the upcoming high-angular resolution radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Our study examines the disk's structure and kinematics, specifically focusing on the inner region where the disk is truncated at approximately 10 AU. We find that the disk's kinematics are consistent with a Keplerian rotation profile, while the disk's structure aligns with a flared geometry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the disk's structure and kinematics can be accurately reproduced by both photoevaporation and MHD disk breeze models. However, we note that the MHD disk breeze model requires a magnetic field strength of approximately 100 G at 10 AU to match the observed kinematics. Finally, we conclude that the upcoming ALMA observations will be instrumental in distinguishing between these two models. This study introduces a hybrid encoding scheme designed for multi-group broadcasting within millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems. The proposed method combines a group-specific codebook with a group-common codebook to enable the transmission of distinct data streams to multiple user groups. To facilitate this, a joint optimization framework is developed to determine the optimal codebooks and precoders for both groups. Simulation results demonstrate that the hybrid encoding approach achieves superior performance compared to conventional single-group broadcasting techniques. Furthermore, the proposed scheme exhibits robustness against channel estimation errors, maintaining high performance even under significant estimation inaccuracies. Additionally, the method is highly scalable, allowing for the simultaneous transmission of data to a large number of user groups. These findings indicate that the hybrid encoding scheme is a promising solution for multi-group broadcasting in mmWave systems. This study addresses two-stage robust optimization problems where the uncertainty set is defined by binary variables. We introduce a Lagrangian dual approach that decomposes the problem into a master problem and a subproblem. The master problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program, while the subproblem is solved using a branch-and-bound algorithm. We demonstrate that the Lagrangian dual provides a lower bound for the original problem and that the Lagrangian dual gap converges to zero as the number of iterations increases. Furthermore, we establish that the Lagrangian dual gap is zero when the number of binary variables is less than or equal to the number of scenarios. Finally, we present numerical results comparing the performance of the Lagrangian dual approach against the standard Benders decomposition method. The findings indicate that the Lagrangian dual approach is more efficient than Benders decomposition for problems with a small number of binary variables. However, for problems with a large number of binary variables, the Lagrangian dual approach may not be as effective as Benders decomposition. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently gained significant attention for their ability to learn from graph-structured data. However, their performance is often constrained by the scarcity of labeled data, which is a common issue in many real-world applications. To address this, we investigate transfer learning within GNNs, specifically examining how to leverage knowledge from a source graph to enhance performance on a target graph. We evaluate various transfer learning strategies, including feature-based, parameter-based, and architecture-based approaches. Our findings indicate that transfer learning can substantially boost GNN performance, particularly when the source and target graphs share similar structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that architecture-based transfer learning is especially effective for GNNs, as it enables the reuse of learned graph structures. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and limitations of transfer learning in GNNs. We present a theoretical framework for intermodal Brillouin scattering in solid-core photonic crystal fibers, which are increasingly utilized in high-power fiber lasers and amplifiers. These findings are crucial for the DUNE collaboration, as they will enable the determination of the Majorana nature of neutrinos and the measurement of the effective Majorana mass. Additionally, the proposed method offers a novel approach to investigating the Majorana nature of neutrinos, distinct from the traditional double-beta decay method. This study is part of the DUNE collaboration's broader effort to explore the Majorana nature of neutrinos. We introduce a method for calculating the point spread function (PSF) of a combined image, which is essential for accurately modeling the PSF in image subtraction. This approach is particularly valuable for subtracting images from different epochs, such as those from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The method is straightforward to implement and can be applied to any combination of images. We demonstrate its application to HST and JWST images of the galaxy NGC 4414. The resulting PSF is highly accurate, with a maximum relative error of 0.001. We investigate how stellar activity influences low-resolution transit spectroscopy and evaluate the effectiveness of high-resolution spectroscopy in mitigating these effects. These results underscore the critical role of high-resolution spectroscopy in future exoplanet transit spectroscopy missions. Finally, we apply this correction to the low-resolution transit spectroscopy of GJ 1151, revealing that the planet's atmosphere is dominated by water vapor. This study highlights the necessity of accounting for stellar activity in low-resolution transit spectroscopy and demonstrates that high-resolution spectroscopy can significantly mitigate these effects. This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling robustness in cyber-physical systems (CPS) by leveraging Signal Temporal Logic (STL). We define robustness as the degree to which a system's behavior adheres to a specified STL formula, even when subjected to disturbances. To achieve this, we propose a new robustness metric that quantifies the extent to which a system's trajectory satisfies an STL formula under disturbance. We demonstrate that this metric is robustly continuous and can be computed efficiently. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this metric in the context of a CPS. The primary contributions of this work are: (1) a new robustness metric for STL formulas, (2) a proof of its robust continuity, and (3) an efficient algorithm for its computation. Additionally, we provide a case study demonstrating the metric's utility in a CPS scenario. The source code for the proposed algorithm is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1995/robustness.

We present a stacking analysis of compact dim radio sources (CDRSs) from the FIRST survey, utilizing the 1.4 GHz NVSS catalog to identify potential counterparts. Our study examines the relationship between angular size and flux density for these sources, revealing that the majority of CDRSs are compact, with 80% having angular sizes smaller than 10 arcsec. This study investigates the statistical strength and prediction accuracy of resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) across multiple brain sites. The proposed method for estimating statistical strength is applicable to any rsFC analysis, including those utilizing machine learning techniques. We introduce a power-saving naming protocol for beeping networks, where nodes communicate by emitting short, silent, or beep signals. In this framework, nodes are assigned unique identifiers from a set of size $n$, and the protocol's objective is to ensure that every node eventually learns the IDs of all other nodes. We demonstrate that a randomized protocol can achieve this goal with high probability using only $O(\log n)$ beeps per node. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ beeps per node, proving that our protocol is asymptotically optimal. Additionally, we show that a deterministic protocol can accomplish the same task with $O(\log^2 n)$ beeps per node. Finally, we extend our results to scenarios where nodes possess only partial knowledge of the total number of nodes. The proofs rely on a novel application of the Lovász Local Lemma. This suppression mechanism may also account for the absence of nematicity in other iron-based superconductors. Finally, we suggest that the nematic instability in LiFeAs could be induced by applying a magnetic field. This proposal is motivated by the fact that the magnetic instability in LiFeAs is suppressed by a magnetic field, and the nematic instability in other iron-based superconductors is also suppressed by a magnetic field. This suggests that the nematic instability in LiFeAs is closely linked to the magnetic instability. The proposed mechanism for inducing the nematic instability in LiFeAs via a magnetic field could provide a new method for investigating the nematic instability in iron-based superconductors. Additionally, this mechanism may offer insights into the relationship between the nematic instability and the superconducting transition temperature in iron-based superconductors. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the nematic instability in iron-based superconductors and may guide future research in this field. This effect is particularly significant in antiferromagnetic insulators, where magnon-magnon interactions are strong and magnon lifetimes are long. We demonstrate that this nonlinear spectral displacement can be detected using a magnon interferometer. Furthermore, we show that the nonlinear spectral displacement of magnons in antiferromagnetic insulators is comparable to that in superconductors. This finding suggests that magnon thermal compression in antiferromagnetic insulators could serve as a viable alternative to the thermal compression of Cooper pairs in superconductors. Additionally, we propose that magnon thermal compression in antiferromagnetic insulators may be utilized to generate squeezed magnon states. Finally, we outline potential applications of magnon thermal compression in antiferromagnetic insulators for magnon-based quantum information processing. Our findings offer a new perspective on magnon thermal compression in antiferromagnetic insulators and provide a foundation for future research in this area. This paper introduces two modifications to the original system: the first involves a specific alteration of the Goppa code, while the second applies a transformation to the quasi-cyclic code. We demonstrate that both alterations are secure against the Information Set Decoding (ISD) attack. Furthermore, we provide a concrete implementation of the system using the first alteration, achieving a security level of 128 bits with a public key size of 1.25 KB. Finally, we outline a potential future direction for this research. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Two-alterations-for-Loidreau's-code-based-cryptosystem. Vertical federated learning (VFL) is a privacy-preserving machine learning framework designed to train models across multiple parties holding distinct data subsets. This paper introduces a novel attack targeting VFL, termed the "pragmatic privacy assault," which exploits the inherent privacy limitations of the framework. The attack operates by leveraging the fact that VFL models are trained on data from only a subset of parties, allowing an adversary to infer sensitive information about the remaining parties. We demonstrate the attack's efficacy through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it can successfully recover private data with high accuracy. Furthermore, we propose a defense mechanism to mitigate this threat. Our findings indicate that the proposed defense significantly reduces the attack's success rate, thereby enhancing the overall privacy of VFL. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively reduces the influence of label noise, thereby enhancing the performance of document ranking. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used for node classification, yet they typically require extensive labeled data. We demonstrate that this method significantly boosts performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we show that our approach outperforms existing pseudo-labeling techniques for GNNs. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence. The AWAKE experiment at CERN investigates the feasibility of using a proton-driven plasma wakefield accelerator to achieve high-energy electron beams. This study presents a simulation analysis of betatron radiation generated by electrons within the plasma wakefield, a phenomenon that could serve as a diagnostic tool for the AWAKE Run 2 experiment. The analysis utilizes the PIC code WARP to model the plasma wakefield and the electron beam, while the radiation is calculated using the analytical formula derived by S. S. Bulanov et al. The results indicate that the radiation spectrum is predominantly concentrated in the soft X-ray range, with a peak intensity of approximately 100 photons per electron per second. Furthermore, the radiation spectrum exhibits a dependence on the plasma density, which can be utilized to determine the plasma density profile. Finally, the study examines the potential for detecting this radiation using a scintillator. The findings suggest that a scintillator with a thickness of 1 cm and a length of 10 cm could detect roughly 100 photons per electron per second. Additionally, the radiation spectrum is observed to be sensitive to the electron beam's energy spread, offering a method to measure the energy spread of the electron beam. These results demonstrate that betatron radiation can be effectively used to diagnose the plasma wakefield and the electron beam in the AWAKE Run 2 experiment. The analysis was conducted using the WARP code, which is available at https://github.com/awake-cern/warp. This work examines the damped inertial mechanics model featuring vanishing Tikhonov regularization, which serves as a continuous-time counterpart to the forward-backward algorithm. We demonstrate that the system's trajectories converge strongly to the minimal norm solution of the underlying monotone inclusion problem. Furthermore, we establish that the trajectories of the associated dual system converge weakly to the minimal norm solution of the dual problem. These findings extend the results of Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019) to the case where the operator is merely monotone. Additionally, we derive a quantitative convergence rate for the primal system and a logarithmic rate for the dual system. Finally, we illustrate the application of these results to the minimal norm solution of a convex optimization problem. The proofs rely on the Lyapunov method and the theory of maximal monotone operators. The primary technical challenge lies in the fact that the operator is not necessarily strongly monotone, which prevents the use of the standard Lyapunov function employed in Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019). Instead, we utilize a specific Lyapunov function that incorporates the squared distance to the minimal norm solution. This approach is inspired by the work of Attouch, Cabot, and Peypouquet (2019) and the paper by Attouch, Cabot, and Redont (2020). The latter study addresses the same problem but under the assumption that the operator is strongly monotone, thereby allowing for the application of the standard Lyapunov function. Consequently, the methodology in Attouch, Cabot, and Redont (2020) cannot be directly applied to the general monotone case. These findings are applicable to various superconductors, including cuprates, iron-based materials, and heavy fermion systems. Additionally, we suggest that the microwave conductivity of doped superconductors can be employed to investigate the nature of the pseudogap. The theoretical predictions derived from this model can be tested through microwave conductivity measurements. We introduce a new class of chiral spin liquids (CSLs) that emerge in amorphous and polycrystalline systems, driven by the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and disorder. In these materials, the CSL phase is stabilized by the competition between the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and the random anisotropy field. We demonstrate that the CSL phase can be realized in a wide range of amorphous and polycrystalline compounds, including spinels, pyrochlores, and perovskites. Furthermore, we show that the CSL phase is robust against disorder and can be tuned by varying the concentration of magnetic ions. Finally, we propose a method to detect the CSL phase in amorphous and polycrystalline systems using neutron scattering. Our findings suggest that the CSL phase is a promising candidate for realizing a topological spin liquid in amorphous and polycrystalline materials. We present the polarized transition matrix component $A_{gq}(N)$ within the variable flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$, which is essential for calculating the polarized gluon distribution at $O(\alpha_s^2)$. This component is derived from the polarized splitting function $P_{gq}(z)$ at $O(\alpha_s^2)$, which itself depends on the polarized quark-to-quark splitting function $P_{qq}(z)$ at $O(\alpha_s^2)$. The calculation involves a two-loop virtual correction and a one-loop real correction. The virtual correction is computed using the method of regions, while the real correction is evaluated via the subtraction method. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (3D+respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) MRI sequence designed for body imaging. The method employs a 3D TSE sequence with a 100% duty cycle, utilizing a 100% duty cycle navigator to track respiratory motion. This navigator data is used to retrospectively sort k-space data into respiratory phases, enabling the reconstruction of 4D images. The sequence was evaluated on 10 healthy volunteers and 10 patients with liver metastases. Results demonstrated that the 4D T2-weighted TSE images provided excellent anatomical detail of the liver and surrounding structures, with no significant motion artifacts. We examine the performance of CountSketch, a randomized dimensionality reduction technique, when applied to adaptive data streams. Specifically, we analyze the scenario where an adversary selects the next data point based on the current sketch. We demonstrate that for any fixed sketch size, there exists an adaptive adversary capable of generating a stream that causes the sketch to fail with high probability. Furthermore, we establish that the sketch size must be at least $\Omega(\log n)$ to ensure success with high probability against such an adaptive adversary. This lower bound is tight, as we present a CountSketch algorithm that succeeds with high probability using a sketch size of $O(\log n)$. Additionally, we extend these findings to the problem of estimating the $k$-th largest element in a stream. Our results indicate that CountSketch can estimate the $k$-th largest element with high probability using a sketch size of $O(k \log n)$ against an adaptive adversary. This bound is also tight, as we prove that any algorithm estimating the $k$-th largest element with high probability requires a sketch size of $\Omega(k \log n)$ in the adaptive setting. Finally, we show that the lower bound of $\Omega(k \log n)$ applies to any algorithm that outputs a set of $k$ elements containing the $k$-th largest element with high probability. This result is tight, as we provide an algorithm that outputs such a set using a sketch size of $O(k \log n)$. These findings are significant because they represent the first lower bounds for adaptive data streams that are tight up to constant factors. Our proofs rely on a novel technique that constructs a specific adaptive adversary to demonstrate the failure of any algorithm with a sketch size smaller than the proposed lower bound. This technique is of independent interest and may be applicable to other problems involving adaptive data streams. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the problem definitions and notation; Section 3 presents the CountSketch algorithm for estimating the mean of a stream; Section 4 provides the lower bound for the mean estimation problem; Section 5 addresses the problem of estimating the $k$-th largest element; and Section 6 concludes the paper. The appendix contains the proofs for the results presented in the main text. This study introduces a context-sensitive computational approach to assess vocal entrainment within dyadic dialogues. The method utilizes a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to model the temporal dynamics of vocal features, specifically pitch and intensity, in both speakers. By employing a two-stage HMM framework, the model first identifies the speaker's current state and subsequently estimates the probability of the other speaker transitioning into that state. This process is repeated across all possible states to calculate the likelihood of the other speaker entering the current state. The resulting metric quantifies the degree of vocal entrainment between the two participants. The proposed method was evaluated using a dataset of 100 dyadic dialogues, where the number of HMM states was optimized to maximize the correlation between the computed entrainment scores and human ratings. The findings demonstrate that the method effectively captures vocal entrainment in dyadic interactions. Furthermore, the study reveals that the optimal number of HMM states varies depending on the specific vocal features being analyzed. Finally, the research indicates that the proposed method can detect vocal entrainment even when the two speakers are not directly interacting. These results suggest that the method holds significant potential for advancing research into vocal entrainment in dyadic dialogues. This outflow is most intense in the central region and extends to the periphery of the [O III] disk. The outflow's morphology aligns with the UV continuum, suggesting that the outflowing gas is primarily ionized by young, massive stars. Furthermore, the outflow exhibits a velocity gradient of approximately 10 km/s/kpc, indicating that the gas is being accelerated by the expanding stellar wind. We introduce a new method for estimating Kendall's tau, a measure of rank correlation, which is particularly effective for large datasets. This approach is grounded in the observation that Kendall's tau can be expressed as a ratio of two U-statistics. By applying a specific approximation to the denominator, we derive a closed-form estimator that is both computationally efficient and asymptotically equivalent to the original statistic. We demonstrate that this estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and we provide a closed-form expression for its asymptotic variance. Furthermore, we show that the estimator is robust against outliers and performs well in finite samples. Finally, we illustrate the method's utility through a simulation study and an application to a real-world dataset. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lewisjones1992/tau.

Furthermore, the planet's frigid environment makes it a prime candidate for studying the atmospheres of cold super-Earths. Future observations of this system will be crucial for characterizing the planet's atmosphere and determining its formation history. Canopus is a consensus protocol designed for asynchronous networks that tolerates up to $f$ Byzantine faults, where $f$ is less than one-third of the total nodes. It achieves this by leveraging a novel Byzantine quorum intersection property. This paper introduces RCanopus, a robust variant of Canopus that maintains the same fault tolerance while offering enhanced resilience against network failures. RCanopus ensures that the system remains operational even if a significant portion of the network is compromised, provided that a majority of the remaining nodes are non-faulty. The protocol's design is straightforward, and its implementation is efficient, requiring only a single message per node per round. Furthermore, RCanopus is provably optimal in terms of message complexity. The protocol's correctness is established through a rigorous proof, and its performance is validated via extensive simulations. The Pierre Auger Observatory, situated in Argentina, is a hybrid detector designed to investigate ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) with energies exceeding $10^{17}$ eV. This study presents a catalog of the most energetic UHECRs recorded during the first phase of the observatory's operation, spanning from 2004 to 2010. The catalog includes 100 events with energies above $10^{19}$ eV and 10 events surpassing $10^{20}$ eV. For each event, the analysis provides the reconstructed energy, arrival direction, and the number of detected particles. Additionally, the study examines the distribution of arrival directions and the energy spectrum of these events. The catalog is accessible at http://www.auger.org/science/analysis/energy/energy_catalog.html. The data presented here are derived from the first phase of the observatory's operation, which concluded in 2010. The second phase, which began in 2010, is expected to yield a catalog of the most energetic cosmic rays with energies above $10^{19}$ eV by the end of 2018. This study examines the capture of cosmic ray particles at low Earth orbits (LEO) using Monte Carlo simulations. The analysis focuses on the energy spectra of captured particles, specifically those with energies exceeding 100 MeV. The results indicate that the energy spectrum of captured particles is significantly harder than that of the primary cosmic ray spectrum. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the energy spectrum of captured particles is largely independent of the specific LEO altitude. Finally, the research highlights that the energy spectrum of captured particles is primarily determined by the energy spectrum of the primary cosmic rays. These findings are crucial for designing shielding systems for satellites and space stations. Additionally, the study suggests that the energy spectrum of captured particles can be utilized to estimate the energy spectrum of primary cosmic rays. The interstellar medium (ISM) is a complex mixture of gas and dust, with dust grains ranging from submicron to micron-sized particles. These grains are responsible for the extinction, emission, and polarization of starlight. While the dense ISM is well-characterized, the sparse ISM remains poorly understood. This study introduces the Astrodust+PAH model, a comprehensive framework for representing the extinction, emission, and polarization of starlight caused by dust in the sparse ISM. The model integrates the properties of dust grains, including their size, shape, composition, and spatial distribution, to accurately simulate the observed characteristics of starlight. By employing a Monte Carlo simulation, the model generates synthetic extinction, emission, and polarization curves for a range of dust properties. These synthetic curves are then compared with observational data to constrain the properties of dust in the sparse ISM. The results indicate that the sparse ISM contains a diverse population of dust grains, with sizes ranging from submicron to micron and compositions varying from carbonaceous to silicate. Furthermore, the study reveals that the spatial distribution of dust in the sparse ISM is highly inhomogeneous, with significant variations in density and structure. Overall, the Astrodust+PAH model offers a robust and versatile tool for investigating the properties of dust in the sparse ISM, thereby enhancing our comprehension of the ISM's role in the formation and evolution of stars and galaxies. The Lights Out game involves a grid of lights where pressing any cell toggles its state and the states of its orthogonal neighbors. This paper examines the Maximum Clicks Dilemma, which asks for the minimum number of clicks required to turn all lights off, given that the game is solvable. We demonstrate that for any solvable configuration on an $n \times n$ grid, the optimal solution requires at most $n^2 - n + 1$ clicks. Furthermore, we prove that for every $n \geq 2$, there exists a solvable configuration on an $n \times n$ grid that necessitates exactly $n^2 - n + 1$ clicks. Finally, we establish that the maximum number of clicks needed to solve a solvable configuration on an $n \times n$ grid is $n^2 - n + 1$ if $n$ is even, and $n^2 - n + 2$ if $n$ is odd. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to determine the minimum number of clicks for any solvable configuration. The paper also includes a section on the history of the game and a discussion of its variants. The source code for the algorithm is available at https://github.com/robertk1998/Maximum-Clicks-Dilemma-in-Lights-Out. The authors thank the anonymous reviewers for their valuable feedback. This study introduces a novel image partitioning model that integrates image reconstruction techniques. The proposed approach is grounded in a variational framework, where the image is segmented into two distinct regions: one representing the background and the other the object. The model's objective function comprises two components: a data fidelity term that ensures the reconstructed image aligns with the observed data, and a regularization term that enforces smoothness within each region. The resulting optimization problem is solved using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed model effectively segments images and reconstructs them with high accuracy. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against noise and can be extended to handle multiple objects. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan1992/Partitioning.

We examine the interaction between a two-level atom and a slender mirror, where the mirror's dimensions are comparable to the atom's excitation wavelength. By employing a Green's function approach, we calculate the atom's excitation probability and the electromagnetic field emitted by the atom-mirror system. Our findings indicate that the atom's excitation probability is significantly enhanced when the mirror is positioned at a distance of approximately half the excitation wavelength. Furthermore, the emitted electromagnetic field exhibits a strong dependence on the mirror's geometry. These results are validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the atom's excitation probability can be modulated by adjusting the mirror's position. This study offers a theoretical framework for investigating atom-mirror interactions in the context of nanophotonics. This study examines the dynamics of a financial bubble, defined as a self-reinforcing process where the expected future price exceeds the current price. We introduce a model featuring a random mean-reverting termination time, which is independent of the bubble's price. The bubble's price follows a geometric Brownian motion with a positive drift, and the termination time is modeled as a random variable with a probability density function. We derive the probability density function for the bubble's price at any given time and analyze the bubble's expected value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bubble's expected value is a convex function of time, implying that the bubble's expected growth rate is non-decreasing. Finally, we propose a diagnostic test for financial bubbles based on the non-decreasing nature of the bubble's expected growth rate. The human brain's ability to recognize objects is a fundamental aspect of cognition, yet the neural mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear. While the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is widely recognized as the primary site for object recognition, the specific neural representations within this region are still debated. This study investigates the neural representations of animacy in the human VTC using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 100 participants. We employed a machine learning approach to decode animacy from fMRI signals and applied a representational similarity analysis (RSA) to examine the relationship between animacy representations and the functional architecture of the VTC. Our findings indicate that animacy representations are distributed across the entire VTC, with a stronger presence in the anterior regions. Furthermore, we observed a significant correlation between the strength of these representations and the functional connectivity of the VTC with the default mode network. These results suggest that animacy representations are not confined to a single area but are instead distributed throughout the VTC, with anterior regions playing a more critical role. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of the VTC's functional connectivity with the default mode network in animacy processing. Overall, this research offers new insights into the neural mechanisms of object recognition and the functional organization of the VTC. This study investigates the evolution of the corona in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571 by analyzing type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed with the Insight-HXMT satellite. The source was monitored for 10.5 days during its 2019 outburst, with data from the 1.5–10 keV energy band used to identify type-C QPOs. The QPO centroid frequency ($
u_{m QPO}$) was determined using the Lomb-Scargle periodogram, while the fractional root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude was calculated via the $\chi^2$ method. The resulting $
u_{m QPO}$ and RMS values were then fitted with a double power-law model to examine the corona's development. Our findings indicate that the corona's structure in MAXI J1535-571 is complex, characterized by a high-energy component with a power-law index of $\Gamma_{m high} = 1.61 \pm 0.02$ and a low-energy component with $\Gamma_{m low} = 2.11 \pm 0.02$. Furthermore, the corona's evolution is linked to the source's spectral state, with the high-energy component dominating during the hard state and the low-energy component becoming more prominent in the soft state. Additionally, the $
u_{m QPO}$ and RMS values exhibit a positive correlation, suggesting that the corona's evolution is driven by the accretion rate. Finally, we propose that the corona's development in MAXI J1535-571 is governed by the Comptonization process. These results offer valuable insights into the corona's evolution in black hole X-ray binaries. The Insight-HXMT data utilized in this work are accessible at http://www.hxmt.ac.cn/. This paper examines the convergence rates of von Neumann's ergodic theorem, specifically analyzing the spectral distribution of the operator $T$ and the associated convergence speed. We demonstrate that the convergence speed is determined by the spectral distribution of $T$ and that the theorem's convergence rate is bounded by the spectral distribution of $T$. Furthermore, we establish that the convergence speed is equivalent to the spectral distribution of $T$ when $T$ is a self-adjoint operator. Finally, we provide an example illustrating that the convergence speed is not necessarily equivalent to the spectral distribution of $T$ in the general case. Additionally, we present a counterexample to show that the convergence speed is not necessarily equivalent to the spectral distribution of $T$ even when $T$ is a normal operator. These findings are derived using the spectral theorem for normal operators. The results are significant for the study of von Neumann's ergodic theorem and the spectral theorem for normal operators. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the spectral theorem for normal operators and von Neumann's ergodic theorem; Section 3 investigates the convergence speed of von Neumann's ergodic theorem; and Section 4 offers an example and a counterexample. This study investigates the relationship between various corpus-based metrics of morphological complexity and their ability to predict the complexity of morphological systems. By utilizing the non-uniformity of the random source, we derive a tighter bound on the phase error rate, which directly enhances the secret key rate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through numerical simulations of the BB84 protocol, showing that it yields a higher secret key rate compared to the standard uniform random source. Furthermore, we extend this technique to the continuous-variable QKD protocol, where it also results in an improved secret key rate. Finally, we discuss the potential for further enhancing the secret key rate by incorporating the non-uniformity of the random source into the phase error rate estimation. This paper introduces a novel non-coherent differential detection method for continuous phase modulation (CPM) that leverages the inherent delay of the channel. The proposed approach is straightforward to implement and achieves performance comparable to the optimal coherent detector. Additionally, it offers a significant advantage over traditional non-coherent differential detection by reducing the required delay to a single symbol period. The study also examines the impact of channel delay on the performance of this new detector. Furthermore, the paper presents a new non-coherent differential detector for CPM that utilizes a delay of $2T$, where $T$ represents the symbol duration. This alternative detector is particularly advantageous when the channel delay is shorter than $T$. The performance of both proposed detectors is evaluated through computer simulations. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the proposed non-coherent differential detector can be effectively applied to CPM signals with a modulation index of $h=1/2$. The findings are validated using a specific example of a CPM signal with $h=1/2$ and a pulse shape defined by $g(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sin(\frac{\pi t}{T})$ for $0\leq t\leq T$. The results indicate that the proposed detector outperforms the traditional non-coherent differential detector, which relies on a delay of $2T$. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. We introduce a topological edge phase in a frustrated Toric code model, which is a spin-1/2 system defined on a square lattice with plaquette interactions. This phase is characterized by a nontrivial topological invariant, specifically the Chern number, and is protected by a symmetry that remains unbroken at the edge. The model's Hamiltonian is derived from a lattice gauge theory featuring a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge group and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ global symmetry. We demonstrate that the topological edge phase emerges when the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ global symmetry is spontaneously broken. Furthermore, we show that the topological edge phase is robust against perturbations that preserve the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ global symmetry. Finally, we propose a method to detect the topological edge phase using a local order parameter. We examine random band matrices featuring intricate deformations, where the deformation matrix is defined as a sum of a few random matrices with large norms. We demonstrate that the sigma-model approximation remains valid for these matrices, provided the band width is sufficiently large. This result extends the findings of [B. Schlein, A. Sznitman, and A. Warzel, Ann. Probab. 45 (2017), 1203--1250] to the case of finite-rank deformations. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a phase transition in the spectral statistics of these matrices. Specifically, we prove that the spectral statistics of the deformed matrices are identical to those of the original random band matrices when the deformation strength is small, whereas they follow Poisson statistics when the deformation strength is large. Additionally, we show that the transition point between these two regimes is determined by the spectral properties of the deformation matrix. Finally, we provide a rigorous derivation of the sigma-model approximation for random band matrices with finite-rank deformations. This derivation relies on the analysis of the resolvent of the deformed matrices, utilizing the resolvent equation and the resolvent identity. The resolvent equation is solved via a fixed-point argument, while the resolvent identity is applied to derive the sigma-model approximation. The validity of the sigma-model approximation is then established by demonstrating that the error term in the approximation is negligible. This approach is applicable to a broad class of random band matrices with finite-rank deformations, encompassing those with independent entries, independent rows, and independent columns. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the model and states the main results; Section 3 outlines the proof strategy; Section 4 presents the proof of the sigma-model approximation; and Section 5 contains the proofs of the main results. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical component of trustworthy machine learning, yet it remains difficult to quantify. This paper introduces a framework for evaluating algorithmic interpretability that is grounded in human learning. We define interpretability as the capacity of a human learner to acquire a model's knowledge through a specific learning process. To measure this, we propose a cognitive intricacy score, which quantifies the difficulty of the learning process. We demonstrate the framework's utility by applying it to decision trees and neural networks. Furthermore, we show that the cognitive intricacy score can be utilized to assess the interpretability of neural networks. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. This study introduces a novel load distribution strategy for virtual machine reservations within cloud data centers, designed to enhance the efficiency of resource allocation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that Prepartition can be effectively integrated with other load distribution methods to further optimize resource allocation. Finally, the study provides a method for selecting the optimal set of sensors to maximize the surveillance system's effectiveness. We present a comprehensive analysis of the masses and distances of unseen companions to five nearby stars exhibiting proper motion acceleration. These stars are located within 100 pc of the Sun and are being monitored by the Gaia mission. Our study utilizes a Bayesian framework to constrain the masses and distances of these companions, incorporating the latest Gaia DR2 data. We also examine the potential impact of the Gaia non-linear astrometric model on our findings. The results indicate that the companions to these stars are likely massive, with a median mass of 1.5 solar masses, and are situated at a median distance of 100 pc. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Gaia non-linear model does not significantly alter our conclusions. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation and evolution of binary systems. We present a parameterized algorithm for determining the upward planarity of a directed graph, with a running time of $O^*(2^k)$, where $k$ represents the number of vertices that are not part of any directed cycle. This approach relies on a novel characterization of upward planarity, which we term the "upward planarity condition." This condition is defined by a set of forbidden subgraphs and is proven to be equivalent to upward planarity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the upward planarity condition can be verified in linear time. The algorithm's efficiency stems from the fact that the upward planarity condition is closed under the operation of contracting a directed cycle. Consequently, the problem can be solved by iteratively contracting directed cycles until the graph is reduced to a single vertex. The number of such contractions is bounded by $k$, and each contraction can be executed in linear time. This study introduces a novel approach for analyzing crowdsourced data, which is often noisy and unreliable. The method employs an ensemble of models to generate a distribution of predictions for each input, thereby quantifying uncertainty. We demonstrate that this distribution can be effectively modeled using a "human softmax" function, which incorporates a temperature parameter to represent the degree of uncertainty. Furthermore, we show that the entropy of this distribution serves as a robust metric for assessing the quality of crowdsourced data. Finally, we illustrate the application of this method in a real-world scenario involving the classification of images from the ImageNet dataset. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robertk1999/Ensemble-Modeling-of-Crowdsourced-Data.

We demonstrate that the norm of the transfer operator for a semiflow on a compact manifold decreases exponentially over time. This result holds under the condition that the semiflow is hyperbolic and possesses a non-trivial stable manifold. Furthermore, we establish that the transfer operator is quasicompact, with its essential spectral radius decaying exponentially. These findings extend the work of Baladi and Tsujii, who previously proved these properties for diffeomorphisms. Additionally, we provide an example of a semiflow that is not hyperbolic yet still exhibits exponential norm diminution. Finally, we examine the implications of these results for the study of the Riemann zeta function. The primary tool employed is the construction of a Lyapunov function. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) involves identifying and segmenting actions within videos. While supervised TAS has achieved significant success, it depends on costly manual annotations. This paper introduces a self-supervised TAS framework that eliminates the need for manual labels. Our approach utilizes a self-supervised co-occurrence activity parsing (SSCAP) module to learn action representations from unlabeled videos. This module employs a self-supervised contrastive learning strategy to capture the co-occurrence relationships between actions and their surrounding contexts. Additionally, we propose a self-supervised temporal action localization (STAL) module to learn action representations from unlabeled videos. The STAL module consists of a temporal action localization (TAL) module and a temporal action recognition (TAR) module, both of which are self-supervised. The TAL module learns action representations by predicting the temporal boundaries of actions, while the TAR module learns them by predicting action classes. Experimental results on the THUMOS14 dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised TAS. We present a theoretical framework for converting spinor atoms into molecules through laser-driven three-body recombination. This process involves the formation of a molecule from two atoms, with the third atom absorbing the released energy. We demonstrate that this mechanism can be utilized to generate molecules in a specific spin state, thereby enabling the creation of spinor molecules. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be extended to produce spinor molecules with a defined total spin. Finally, we outline potential applications of this method in the study of spinor molecules. The proposed scheme is applicable to any atomic species capable of three-body recombination. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the process using rubidium-87 as a concrete example. Our findings indicate that the spinor atom-molecule transformation can be achieved with a conversion efficiency of approximately 10% and a production rate of roughly 100 molecules per second. This method offers a promising avenue for investigating the properties of spinor molecules. This representation is subsequently utilized to predict the entity's future state. Furthermore, we analyze the model's performance across various scenarios, including those involving multiple entities and those with limited historical data. We report the observation of a reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase in a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure at moderate Landau-level-coupling strength, characterized by a filling factor of 5/2. This phase exhibits a distinct energy gap and a non-Abelian topological order, as evidenced by the presence of a fractional charge of e/4 and a non-Abelian anyon. The reentrant nature of this phase is attributed to the interplay between the Landau-level-coupling strength and the Zeeman energy. Our findings suggest that the 5/2 quantum Hall phase is more robust than previously thought, potentially enabling its realization in a broader range of materials. Furthermore, the reentrant 5/2 phase may offer a promising platform for investigating the interplay between non-Abelian topological order and superconductivity. This study addresses the Dial-a-Ride Problem (DARP) within a metropolitan context, where a fleet of vehicles must transport passengers between various locations. The objective is to minimize the total travel time of all vehicles while adhering to specific constraints, such as time windows and vehicle capacity. We introduce a novel Branch-and-Trim algorithm designed to solve this problem. The algorithm's core mechanism involves iteratively solving a relaxed version of the problem and subsequently eliminating infeasible solutions from the search space. This process continues until a feasible solution is identified. The proposed method was evaluated against a standard Branch-and-Bound algorithm using a set of benchmark instances. The results demonstrate that the Branch-and-Trim approach is highly effective, particularly for large-scale problems. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance is robust across different vehicle capacities and time window constraints. Finally, the paper outlines potential future research directions. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative condition that impairs memory and cognitive functions. Early detection is crucial for effective treatment, yet current diagnostic methods often fail to identify the disease in its initial stages. This study introduces a novel approach to predict AD progression using a deep learning model called Deep InfoMax (DIM). The model utilizes a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) to analyze MRI scans, employing a multi-scale strategy to capture both local and global features. Additionally, a multi-task learning framework is implemented to simultaneously predict the disease's progression and the patient's age. The model's performance is evaluated using the ADNI dataset, which includes MRI scans from 1,000 individuals. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a 90% accuracy rate in predicting AD progression. Furthermore, the model successfully predicts patient age with a mean absolute error of 2.5 years. These findings indicate that the proposed method is highly effective for early AD detection and holds significant potential for clinical applications. We introduce a novel biasing potential for molecular dynamics simulations of DNA, termed Stiff Base Biasing (SBB). This method restricts the sampling of base-pair parameters to a narrow region around the equilibrium values of the DNA double helix. By limiting the conformational space of the DNA double helix, SBB enhances the sampling of the remaining degrees of freedom, thereby accelerating the exploration of the DNA conformational landscape. We demonstrate the efficacy of SBB by applying it to a 100 base-pair DNA sequence, which is then utilized to calculate the free energy landscape of the DNA double helix. The results indicate that SBB significantly improves the sampling of DNA conformations compared to unbiased simulations. Furthermore, we show that the free energy landscape derived from SBB simulations aligns well with that obtained from unbiased simulations. Finally, we illustrate how SBB can be employed to identify the most probable DNA conformations. The SBB method is implemented in the open-source software package OpenMM. We demonstrate that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, when analyzed as a three-dimensional random field, provides a direct and immediate constraint on the cosmological matter power spectrum. This approach bypasses the need for intermediate steps such as reconstructing the density field or modeling the bias between the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest and the underlying matter distribution. By utilizing the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, we derive a constraint on the matter power spectrum that is comparable in precision to current limits from the cosmic microwave background. Furthermore, we show that this method can be extended to constrain the growth of structure, thereby offering a novel and independent probe of dark energy. The primary advantage of this technique is its simplicity, which allows for the rapid assessment of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest's potential as a cosmological tool. Additionally, this method is applicable to any three-dimensional random field, including the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, the distribution of galaxies, and the cosmic microwave background. We anticipate that this approach will facilitate the development of new cosmological analyses and the creation of novel statistical tools for the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. This paper introduces the concept of distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds within nearly contact manifolds. We examine the geometric characteristics of these submanifolds and provide specific examples. Furthermore, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for a distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold to be pointwise slant, pointwise anti-invariant, or pointwise invariant. Finally, we demonstrate that a distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold is pointwise slant if and only if it is a distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold of type (1,1). Additionally, we prove that a distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold is pointwise anti-invariant if and only if it is a distorted product pointwise anti-invariant submanifold. We also show that a distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifold is pointwise invariant if and only if it is a distorted product pointwise invariant submanifold. Finally, we present examples of distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds that are neither pointwise slant, pointwise anti-invariant, nor pointwise invariant.

We investigate the dynamics of colloidal particles within activity gradients, where the activity of surrounding active particles varies spatially. Our findings indicate that the effective potential governing the colloidal particle's motion is non-conservative, leading to a non-equilibrium steady state. We demonstrate that the particle's mean position and velocity depend on the gradient of the activity field. Furthermore, we show that the particle's effective temperature is determined by the activity of the surrounding active particles. Finally, we examine the particle's motion in a two-dimensional activity gradient, revealing that the particle's trajectory is influenced by the gradient's orientation. These results offer a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of colloidal particles in activity gradients, which is crucial for designing active matter systems. Additionally, our findings may have implications for the study of biological systems, as cells and other biological entities often exhibit activity gradients. This method is grounded in the concept of a "clustering radius," defined as the maximum distance from a cluster's center to any node within it. We demonstrate that the optimal clustering radius is determined by the network's diameter and the number of outbreaks. We introduce a straightforward method to mitigate the impact of point sources on maximum likelihood CMB maps. This approach involves subtracting the point source signal from the map prior to the maximum likelihood estimation. We demonstrate that this technique is highly effective in reducing the bias introduced by point sources, even when the sources are not perfectly resolved. Furthermore, we show that this method is applicable to both the standard maximum likelihood estimator and the maximum a posteriori estimator. Finally, we illustrate the method's efficacy using simulated data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/PointSourceSubtraction. We introduce a novel approach to address referential ambiguity in language-directed goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. This method employs a goal-conditioned policy that utilizes a language model to generate multiple candidate goals for each instruction, subsequently selecting the most appropriate one through a learned reward function. We demonstrate that this strategy effectively mitigates referential ambiguity and significantly enhances performance on the ALFWorld benchmark. Furthermore, we show that the learned reward function can be leveraged to automatically construct a reward function for a new task, thereby facilitating zero-shot transfer. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/kaist-ai-lab/ambiguity.

We introduce a Bayesian framework for designing adaptive Ramsey sequence measurements, which are widely employed in quantum metrology. This approach enables the sequential determination of optimal measurement settings, thereby maximizing the information gained from each step. We demonstrate that this method surpasses the performance of standard Ramsey sequences and achieves the quantum Cramér-Rao bound. Furthermore, we show that the optimal measurement strategy can be derived analytically. Finally, we apply this technique to a Ramsey sequence measurement of a magnetic field, utilizing a spin-1/2 system. The resulting optimal measurement strategy is compared against a standard Ramsey sequence and a previously proposed adaptive strategy. Our findings indicate that the optimal strategy yields a 1.5-fold improvement in precision over the standard Ramsey sequence and a 1.2-fold improvement over the prior adaptive strategy. Additionally, we observe that the optimal strategy exhibits a distinct behavior compared to the other two approaches. These results suggest that the proposed method could be valuable for enhancing the precision of quantum metrology. Network centrality metrics are essential for identifying influential nodes within a network. While many existing methods rely on shortest-path distances, they often fail to capture the full complexity of network structure. This paper introduces a novel centrality measure called Gromov centrality, which utilizes the Gromov product to quantify the extent to which a node's neighbors cluster together. We demonstrate that this metric is highly sensitive to local network topology and can be computed efficiently. Furthermore, we show that Gromov centrality effectively identifies key nodes in both synthetic and real-world networks. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the metric's properties and its relationship to other centrality measures. This study examines the behavior of discrete-time dynamical systems defined by smooth, strongly monotonic maps on $\mathbb{R}^n$. This study introduces a robust transmission design for secure multiuser communication networks supported by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), specifically addressing hardware imperfections in both the RIS and user equipment. The primary objective is to maximize the minimum secrecy rate across all users. To achieve this, we propose a two-stage algorithm that jointly optimizes the transmit covariance matrix and the RIS phase shifts. In the first stage, the transmit covariance matrix is optimized using a semidefinite relaxation (SDR) approach, while the RIS phase shifts are optimized via a successive convex approximation (SCA) method. In the second stage, the RIS phase shifts are refined using a low-complexity alternating optimization (AO) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed robust design significantly outperforms conventional designs that ignore hardware deficiencies. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm converges rapidly, and its computational complexity is substantially lower than that of the conventional design. Finally, the proposed robust design is shown to be more resilient to hardware deficiencies than the conventional design. These findings indicate that the proposed robust design is highly effective for RIS-supported secure multiuser communication networks. We introduce a new class of Markov chains designed for sampling from a product of measures defined on a product space. These chains are constructed by combining two distinct types of samplers: one that samples from the product of measures and another that samples from a single measure. We demonstrate that the contrast of these chains is bounded by the product of the contrasts of the individual samplers. This result extends the findings of [1] and [2], which were limited to the case where the product of measures consists of identical components. Furthermore, we apply this framework to develop a novel algorithm for sampling from a product of measures, utilizing a step sampler for the product space and a single measure sampler. We prove that the contrast of this new algorithm is bounded by the product of the contrasts of the two samplers. Finally, we illustrate the application of this algorithm to sampling from a product of Gaussian measures.

We introduce a statistical framework for characterizing the time-domain behavior of non-repetitive optical clocks, which are essential for next-generation timekeeping. This approach is grounded in the concept of a clock's "state," defined as the cumulative history of its past outputs. We demonstrate that the clock's output can be modeled as a stochastic process driven by a Markovian evolution of this state. Furthermore, we establish that the clock's output is a Gaussian process, with its statistical properties fully determined by the state's evolution. Finally, we outline a method for estimating the clock's state from its output and show that this estimation can be performed using a Kalman filter. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of a non-repetitive optical clock. The proposed statistical description offers a robust foundation for analyzing the time-domain performance of non-repetitive optical clocks and holds potential for broader applications in timekeeping. Additionally, it provides a framework for developing optimal algorithms to estimate the clock's state from its output. This study investigates how grammatical gender influences the semantic representations of nouns in gender-marking languages. We hypothesize that nouns sharing the same gender are more semantically similar than those with different genders, a pattern we expect to be more pronounced in languages with a larger number of gender categories. To test this, we analyzed 100,000 nouns from 10 languages, including both gender-marking and non-gender-marking varieties. Our findings indicate that nouns within the same gender are indeed more similar than those across genders, and this effect is stronger in languages with more gender categories. Furthermore, we observed that gender similarity is more closely linked to semantic similarity than to phonological similarity. Finally, we demonstrate that gender similarity can be effectively predicted using a language's gender system, suggesting that grammatical gender shapes the semantic representations of nouns. These results offer new insights into the relationship between grammar and semantics. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/linguistics-ai/gender. We introduce a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach designed to emulate fermionic systems. This method leverages the natural evolution of a quantum system under a specific Hamiltonian, which is subsequently corrected by a digital quantum circuit. We demonstrate that this technique can accurately simulate the dynamics of a fermionic system, specifically the one-dimensional Hubbard model, on a quantum computer. Furthermore, we show that the method is capable of calculating the ground state energy of the Hubbard model. Finally, we present a proof of concept for this approach using a quantum computer simulator. The proposed method is expected to be applicable to a broad range of fermionic systems. Additionally, we anticipate that this hybrid digital-analog quantum computing strategy will facilitate the emulation of fermionic systems on near-term quantum computers. The ALICE Collaboration presents the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of charged particles originating from beauty-hadron decays, measured in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. This analysis utilizes the dimuon decay channel of beauty hadrons, with $v_2$ determined via the two-particle correlation method. The study covers a transverse momentum range of 2.0 < $p_{\rm T}$ < 10.0 GeV/$c$ and an azimuthal angle range of $|\eta|$ < 0.8. The results indicate that the $v_2$ of beauty-hadron decay products is positive and increases with $p_{\rm T}$, a trend consistent with the $v_2$ observed for charged particles from light-flavor hadron decays. This work examines the GDoF performance of $K$-user interference networks under two distinct power control strategies: binary power control, where each user transmits at either full or zero power, and optimal power control, which allows for continuous power adjustments. We demonstrate that the GDoF advantage of optimal power control over binary control scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding is significant because it reveals that the GDoF gain from optimal power control is substantial, thereby challenging the common assumption that binary power control is sufficient for achieving optimal GDoF. Furthermore, we establish that the GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control is at least $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ for any $K$-user interference network. This lower bound is derived by analyzing a specific $K$-user interference network where the GDoF gain is exactly $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. The analysis of this network relies on a novel outer bound for the GDoF region of $K$-user interference networks, which is based on the concept of "interference alignment with interference leakage." This new outer bound is also of independent interest. Finally, we show that the GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control is at most $O(\sqrt{K})$ for any $K$-user interference network. This upper bound is achieved by constructing a specific $K$-user interference network where the GDoF gain is exactly $O(\sqrt{K})$. The construction of this network utilizes a new inner bound for the GDoF region of $K$-user interference networks, which is based on the concept of "interference alignment with interference leakage." This new inner bound is also of independent interest. The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model and the problem formulation. Section III presents the main results. Section IV provides the proof of the lower bound on the GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control. Section V provides the proof of the upper bound on the GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control. Section VI concludes the paper. Appendix A contains the proof of the outer bound for the GDoF region of $K$-user interference networks, and Appendix B contains the proof of the inner bound for the GDoF region of $K$-user interference networks.

This paper introduces a novel approach to compliance verification for trace segments, which are subsequences of event logs. We define a new alignment concept called infix alignment, which is more general than the standard alignment used in process mining. This concept is then applied to compliance checking, where a trace segment is deemed compliant if it can be aligned with a process model without violating any rules. We demonstrate that infix alignment is equivalent to postfix alignment, a concept previously introduced in the literature. Furthermore, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing infix alignments and prove that the resulting compliance verification problem is NP-complete. Finally, we provide a case study illustrating the application of our method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ProcessMiningGroup/ComplianceVerification.

Keywords: Compliance verification, trace segments, infix alignment, postfix alignment, process mining.

Colloidal gels are widely utilized in industrial applications, yet their mechanical and flow properties are often difficult to control. This study demonstrates that applying ultrasonic vibrations to colloidal gels can significantly alter their rheological behavior. Specifically, we show that these vibrations can either stiffen or soften the gel structure, depending on the frequency and amplitude of the applied sound. Furthermore, we observe that the gel's yield stress can be tuned by adjusting the vibration parameters. These findings suggest that ultrasonic vibrations offer a promising method for regulating the mechanical and flow characteristics of colloidal gels. The underlying mechanism is attributed to the vibration-induced modification of the gel's microstructure. Our results provide a new approach for tailoring the properties of colloidal gels for specific industrial uses. Additionally, we propose that this technique could be applied to other soft matter systems, such as foams and emulsions, to adjust their mechanical and flow properties. Ultimately, this research opens up new avenues for the design and optimization of colloidal gels and other soft matter systems. If $n$ is even, the sequence is $n, n/2, \dots$, and by the inductive hypothesis, this sequence eventually reaches 1. If $n$ is odd, the sequence is $n, 3n+1, \dots$, and by the inductive hypothesis, this sequence eventually reaches 1. Thus, the conjecture holds for all positive integers. The proof is complete. This paper serves as a sequel to [10], where we established the PBW basis for Nichols algebras associated with traditional Weyl groups. In this work, we demonstrate that the Nichols algebra of a traditional Weyl group is isomorphic to the Nichols algebra of a specific braided vector space. Furthermore, we provide a classification of these Nichols algebras. As a consequence, we derive a classification of Nichols algebras of rank 2 over traditional Weyl groups. Additionally, we prove that the Nichols algebra of a traditional Weyl group is finite-dimensional if and only if it is isomorphic to the Nichols algebra of a braided vector space of type $A_1 \times A_1$. Finally, we show that the Nichols algebra of a traditional Weyl group is isomorphic to the Nichols algebra of a braided vector space of type $A_1 \times A_1$ precisely when the traditional Weyl group is of type $B_2$ or $G_2$. This result extends the findings of [11] and [12]. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background material. Section 3 presents the main results. Section 8 contains the proofs for the results in Section 7. Finally, Section 9 outlines the classification of Nichols algebras of type $A_1 \times A_1$.

We present a comprehensive study of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, utilizing both exact diagonalization and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings reveal that the system exhibits a rich phase diagram characterized by a sequence of symmetry-broken phases, including a $120^\circ$ ordered state, a $60^\circ$ ordered state, and a $30^\circ$ ordered state. Additionally, we identify a distinct liquid phase that emerges at intermediate interaction strengths. This liquid phase is marked by a significant reduction in the spin gap and a substantial increase in the spin stiffness. We further demonstrate that the $30^\circ$ ordered phase is a spin-liquid state, evidenced by the absence of long-range order in the spin-spin correlation function and the presence of a finite spin gap. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the dynamical properties of the system, highlighting the unique characteristics of the liquid phase. These results offer valuable insights into the behavior of frustrated quantum magnets and may have implications for the development of new quantum materials. We investigate the restriction-derestriction transition within $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which occurs when the Higgs field's vacuum expectation value (VEV) magnitude crosses a critical threshold. This transition is characterized by a shift from a restricted phase, where the Higgs VEV is confined to a specific subgroup, to a derestricted phase where it is no longer so. We demonstrate that this transition is of first order, evidenced by a discontinuity in the Higgs VEV and the emergence of a latent heat. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of the Higgs VEV near the critical point, revealing that it follows a power law with an exponent of $1/2$. Finally, we examine the implications of this transition for the electroweak phase transition. Our findings indicate that the transition is strongly first order, thereby supporting the viability of electroweak baryogenesis. Additionally, we show that the critical temperature for this transition is approximately $100$ GeV, which aligns with the electroweak scale. These results suggest that the restriction-derestriction transition could play a significant role in the early universe's evolution. This study introduces a nonparametric estimator for conditional expectation functions, which are defined as the expected values of a response variable given a vector of covariates. The proposed estimator is constructed by applying a kernel function to the conditional expectation function. We demonstrate that this estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic normality of the estimator's derivative and provide a simulation study to evaluate its performance. Finally, we apply the estimator to analyze the relationship between the number of hours worked and the logarithm of hourly wages. The results indicate that the conditional expectation function is non-monotonic, suggesting that the relationship between work hours and wages is not straightforward. Additionally, the derivative of the function is negative for most values of the covariates, implying that increasing work hours generally leads to a decrease in hourly wages. These findings align with the economic theory of diminishing marginal returns. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the estimator and its asymptotic properties; Section 3 details the simulation study; Section 4 applies the estimator to the wage data; and Section 5 offers concluding remarks. We introduce a micro-fabricated deep silicon atomic vapor chamber designed for the study of atomic physics. This device features a 100 $\mu$m thick silicon substrate with a 100 $\mu$m deep trench etched into it, which is subsequently filled with a cesium vapor. The trench is sealed using a silicon wafer bonded to the substrate via anodic bonding. The resulting chamber measures 100 $\mu$m in height, 100 $\mu$m in width, and 10 mm in length. We demonstrate that the chamber can be filled with cesium vapor at a pressure of 100 mbar, and we report the measured absorption spectrum of the cesium vapor. Furthermore, we show that the chamber can be integrated with a silicon photonic waveguide. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this device in atomic physics research. The fabrication process is detailed in the accompanying manuscript. This study introduces a novel deep learning-based infrared-visible fusion method designed to enhance the visual quality of infrared imagery for wildfire monitoring. The proposed technique, named FIRe-GAN, leverages the generative capabilities of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate high-fidelity infrared images. Experimental results demonstrate that FIRe-GAN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness across various datasets and is capable of producing high-quality infrared images even when the input visible images are of low resolution. This study introduces a stochastic compartmental model designed to simulate the transmission dynamics of COVID-19. The model incorporates a random component to account for the inherent uncertainty in the disease's spread. We analyze the model's stability and demonstrate that the stochastic system converges to a unique stationary distribution. Furthermore, we derive the basic reproduction number, denoted as $R_0$, and establish the conditions under which the disease-free equilibrium is stochastically stable. Finally, we apply the model to real-world data from the United States to estimate the values of $R_0$ and the transmission rate. The findings indicate that the stochastic model aligns well with the observed data. Additionally, we examine the impact of various interventions on the disease's transmission. The results suggest that interventions such as social distancing, quarantine, and isolation are effective in reducing the transmission rate. However, the study also highlights that the transmission rate is highly sensitive to the initial conditions of the system. Consequently, we recommend that policymakers implement these interventions early in the outbreak to effectively control the spread of the disease. The source code for the model is available at https://github.com/AbdullahAlshammari/COVID-19. The data used in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/AbdullahAlshammari/COVID-19-Data. Section 4 applies the model to real-world data, and Section 5 concludes the study. Finally, Section 6 provides the proofs for the theorems presented in the paper.

This study examines a feedback-regulated system featuring Coulomb resistance, where the resistance force is proportional to the sign of the velocity. We demonstrate that the system's state converges to a limit cycle, which may be either a fixed point or a periodic orbit. Furthermore, we establish that the system exhibits stick-slip behavior if and only if the limit cycle is a periodic orbit. Finally, we derive a sufficient condition for the existence of a periodic orbit. The analysis relies on the theory of differential inclusions and the properties of monotone operators. The findings are illustrated through a numerical example. This research extends the work of [1], which addressed a similar problem but without Coulomb resistance. The primary distinction lies in the fact that the feedback-regulated system with Coulomb resistance is not a differential inclusion with a monotone operator, whereas the system without Coulomb resistance is. Consequently, the proof techniques employed in this paper differ from those in [1].

We demonstrate that the optimal rank-one approximation is characterized by a specific limit, which we term the essential limit. This concept is defined as the limit of the empirical distribution of the rows, where the empirical distribution is constructed by assigning each row a weight equal to the inverse of its distribution's density evaluated at that row.
